items.explanation: CREEP's 1972 campaign of political sabotage included break-ins, IRS audits of 'enemies,' and obstructing justice — but falsifying an opponent's war record wasn't among them.
options: A. Breaking into private offices
B. Using IRS records against 'enemies'
C. Falsifying opponents' war records
D. Obstructing investigations of campaign aides
items.stem: Which tactic was NOT used by Nixon's 1972 campaign?

option_explanations.A: CREEP really did break into private offices — the Watergate break-in was the most famous, but there were others. This was a real 1972 campaign tactic, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The 1972 campaign really did use IRS records against 'enemies' — the enemies list and tax audits were real. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. CREEP's 1972 methods included break-ins, IRS audits of 'enemies,' and obstructing justice — but falsifying an opponent's war record was not among them.
option_explanations.D: The 1972 campaign really did obstruct investigations of its aides — the Watergate cover-up was exactly that. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Supply-siders claimed tax cuts for the wealthy would be reinvested — in factories, stocks, and expansion — rather than hoarded; the theory's critics said savings just piled up.
options: A. Invest heavily in the economy
B. Open new factories
C. Buy stocks
D. Dramatically increase their savings
items.stem: Supply-side economics held that wealthy tax-cut recipients would do all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Supply-siders really did claim the wealthy would invest heavily in the economy — that was the theory's promise. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Supply-siders really did claim new factories would open — investment in productive enterprise was the promised mechanism. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Supply-siders really did expect stock purchases — investment through the markets was part of the promised reinvestment. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. Supply-siders claimed tax cuts for the wealthy would be reinvested — in factories, stocks, and expansion — rather than hoarded. Dramatically increasing savings was what critics said would actually happen, not what the theory promised.

items.explanation: Reagan-era deficits came from slashed tax rates, soaring military budgets, and loopholes for the wealthy — not from education spending, which stagnated despite urban schools' desperate needs.
options: A. Reduced federal tax rates
B. Surging education funding
C. Higher military spending
D. Tax-code favors for the wealthy
items.stem: Which did NOT contribute to Reagan-era deficits?

option_explanations.A: Reduced federal tax rates really did contribute to Reagan-era deficits — the 1981 cuts slashed revenue. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. Surging education funding did not cause the deficits — education spending stagnated despite urban schools' desperate needs. The deficits came from tax cuts, military spending, and loopholes.
option_explanations.C: Higher military spending really did contribute — Reagan's arms buildup exploded the budget. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Tax-code favors for the wealthy really did contribute — loopholes drained revenue. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Reagan's critics grant the tax cuts tamed inflation and his image was golden — but argue the benefits flowed upward while the middle and working classes lost ground.
options: A. The effects of the 1981–83 tax cuts
B. The U.S. response to Libya
C. His policies' effects on the middle and lower classes
D. His public image and political skill

option_explanations.A: Critics did not most emphasize the tax cuts' effects in isolation — they granted the cuts tamed inflation. The core of the critique was distributional: who gained and who lost.
option_explanations.B: The U.S. response to Libya (the 1986 bombing) was not the critics' main emphasis — it was a minor episode compared with the economic critique.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Reagan's critics grant that the tax cuts tamed inflation and that his image was golden — but argue the benefits flowed upward while the middle and working classes lost ground.
option_explanations.D: Critics did not most emphasize his public image and political skill — they conceded those. Their emphasis was on the distributional effects of his policies.

items.explanation: Ford's 'Whip Inflation Now' buttons struck Americans as a PR gimmick — evidence, to many, that he had no real economic program.
options: A. He had no real grasp of economics
B. He brilliantly inspired the public
C. He lived in Nixon's shadow
D. He mastered foreign policy
items.stem: Ford's WIN program convinced many Americans that

option_explanations.A: Correct. Ford's 'Whip Inflation Now' buttons struck Americans as a PR gimmick — enlisting the public to fight inflation with slogans convinced many he had no real economic program.
option_explanations.B: WIN did not brilliantly inspire the public — it was widely mocked as empty symbolism. Inspiration was the opposite of its effect.
option_explanations.C: Living in Nixon's shadow was a real Ford problem, but WIN specifically convinced Americans about his economic grasp — or lack of it — not about Nixon.
option_explanations.D: WIN said nothing about foreign policy — it was a domestic economic gimmick. Ford's foreign policy was a separate matter (Kissinger, Helsinki, the Mayaguez).

items.explanation: Reagan's chain of causation is explicit: raising taxes 'will encourage more government spending and less private investment,' 'slow economic growth, reduce production, and destroy future jobs.' He argues tax hikes grow government and kill jobs -- the opposite of deficit reduction or aid to the jobless.
options: A. Encourage more government spending and destroy jobs
B. Reduce the federal deficit
C. Make it easier for the unemployed to find work
D. Slow the growth of government
items.stem: In the passage, Reagan argues that raising taxes would
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Reagan argued that raising taxes would not shrink deficits: revenues had risen sharply in 1980, he claimed, yet the deficit still hit record highs — proof, in his view, that the problem was runaway spending, not insufficient taxes.
—After President Ronald Reagan, remarks on the economy, early 1980s

option_explanations.A: Correct. Reagan's chain of causation is explicit: raising taxes 'will encourage more government spending and less private investment,' 'slow economic growth, reduce production, and destroy future jobs.' He argues tax hikes grow government and kill jobs.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of Reagan's argument — he claimed raising taxes would NOT reduce the deficit, because the problem was spending, not insufficient revenue.
option_explanations.C: Reagan did not argue tax hikes would help the unemployed find work — he argued they would destroy jobs, making unemployment worse.
option_explanations.D: The opposite of Reagan's argument — he claimed raising taxes would encourage more government spending, not slow it.

items.explanation: Democrats warned -- correctly, as the 1980s proved -- that cutting taxes while exploding military spending would balloon the deficit; the national debt nearly tripled under Reagan. Supply-siders promised growth would pay for the cuts; critics predicted red ink, and got it.
options: A. Cause immediate deflation
B. Explode the federal deficit
C. Strengthen labor unions
D. End the Cold War prematurely
items.stem: Critics of Reagan's tax cuts argued they would
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Reagan argued that raising taxes would not shrink deficits: revenues had risen sharply in 1980, he claimed, yet the deficit still hit record highs — proof, in his view, that the problem was runaway spending, not insufficient taxes.
—After President Ronald Reagan, remarks on the economy, early 1980s

option_explanations.A: Critics did not predict deflation — they predicted the opposite problem: ballooning deficits and debt. Deflation was never their warning.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Democrats warned — correctly, as the 1980s proved — that cutting taxes while exploding military spending would balloon the deficit; the national debt nearly tripled under Reagan. Critics predicted red ink, and got it.
option_explanations.C: Critics did not argue the tax cuts would strengthen labor unions — the cuts had nothing to do with union strength, and unions kept declining in the 1980s.
option_explanations.D: Critics did not argue the tax cuts would end the Cold War prematurely — tax policy and the Cold War's end were separate matters.

items.explanation: Where Nixon and Kissinger pursued detente and Carter stressed human rights, Reagan denounced the USSR as an 'evil empire,' launched a massive arms buildup, and funded anti-communist insurgents from Nicaragua to Afghanistan. It was a deliberate break with accommodation in favor of confrontation and military superiority.
options: A. Reducing American defense spending
B. Recognizing the Soviet Union's permanence
C. Withdrawing the United States from its alliances
D. Seeking confrontation and military superiority rather than accommodation
items.stem: Reagan's foreign policy differed from the detente of Nixon and Carter in
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Reagan argued that raising taxes would not shrink deficits: revenues had risen sharply in 1980, he claimed, yet the deficit still hit record highs — proof, in his view, that the problem was runaway spending, not insufficient taxes.
—After President Ronald Reagan, remarks on the economy, early 1980s

option_explanations.A: Reagan did not reduce American defense spending — he launched a massive arms buildup. Reduction was the opposite of his policy.
option_explanations.B: Reagan did not recognize the Soviet Union's permanence — he called it an 'evil empire' and predicted it would end up on the 'ash heap of history.'
option_explanations.C: Reagan did not withdraw the United States from its alliances — NATO remained central to his strategy. Withdrawal was never his policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Where Nixon and Kissinger pursued detente and Carter stressed human rights, Reagan denounced the USSR as an 'evil empire,' launched a massive arms buildup, and funded anti-communist insurgents from Nicaragua to Afghanistan — a deliberate break with accommodation in favor of confrontation and military superiority.
